riddles.chamberPrompt: Yama tests the boy's resolve: 'Two paths present themselves to every human being: Śreyas (the good) and Preyas (the pleasant). By what mark does the resolute mind choose?'

options.text: The wise inspect both; they choose Śreyas over Preyas because it leads to enduring freedom, whereas the foolish cling to momentary gratification.
options.explanation: Correct. Kaṭha 1.2.2 states: 'tayor śreya ādadānasya sādhu bhavati, hīyate 'rthād ya u preyo vṛṇīte.' He who chooses the good fares well; he who chooses the pleasant misses the true goal.

options.text: The wise avoid all choices entirely and retreat into passive indifference.
options.explanation: Kaṭha rejects numbness: discernment requires active, conscious examination of both paths.

options.text: The wise accumulate vast wealth and power first, seeking spiritual wisdom only at the end of life.
options.explanation: Nachiketa explicitly rejected Yama's offer of gold, herds, and kingdoms, calling them 'ephemeral destroyers of the vigor of the senses' (1.1.26).

options.text: The pleasant and the good are identical, so any sensory pleasure leads naturally to liberation.
options.explanation: Kaṭha 1.2.1 declares that the two paths bind to completely divergent ends.

riddles.doorName: The Second Door of the Chariot
riddles.chamberPrompt: Yama gestures to the carriage: 'Know the Self as the passenger sitting within the chariot. Who is the charioteer holding the reins, and what happens when the reins are slack?'

options.text: The intellect (buddhi) is the charioteer and the mind (manas) is the reins. With undisciplined mind, the sense-horses bolt like wild beasts.
options.explanation: Correct. Kaṭha 1.3.3-4: 'buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi, manaḥ pragraham eva ca.' The intellect must guide the reins of attention.

options.text: The senses are the charioteer, and they should be given complete freedom to steer the body wherever desires wander.
options.explanation: If the senses lead, Kaṭha 1.3.5 warns that the chariot crashes off the road of life.

options.text: The body itself is the charioteer, and physical strength alone guarantees safe passage.
options.explanation: The body is merely the carriage (śarīraṃ ratham eva tu); it requires cognitive governance.

options.text: The horses must be destroyed and starved so the carriage cannot move at all.
options.explanation: The Upanishads do not advocate mortification of the senses, but their intelligent mastery.

riddles.doorName: The Third Door of the Unborn Ground
riddles.chamberPrompt: Yama reveals the supreme mystery: 'When the physical frame collapses at death, what happens to the conscious witness within?'

options.text: The knowing Self is never born and never dies; it sprang from nothing and nothing sprang from it. Unborn, eternal, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
options.explanation: Correct. Kaṭha 1.2.18: 'na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścin... na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre.' That unshakeable ground is the root of Upanishadic resilience.

options.text: Consciousness is extinguished completely into permanent nothingness.
options.explanation: Yama demonstrates that pure consciousness is the ground of existence, not a temporary biological byproduct.

options.text: The Self reincarnates immediately into whatever material possessions it owned during life.
options.explanation: Material possessions do not migrate; only mental impressions (saṃskāras) continue.

options.text: The Self becomes a ghost trapped forever at the door of Yama.
options.explanation: The realization of the Self leads to absolute fearlessness and liberation (mokṣa).
